newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: FEATURE - Silk king mystery intrigues 30 years on. [CORRECTED 06:15 GMT]
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Silk king mystery intrigues 30 years on. [CORRECTED 06:15 GMT]

text.p: Some say he was eaten by a tiger and some even say he was swallowed by a snake. Others think he was kidnapped by communists or an aborigine girl to be her (corrects from his) "love slave".
Many think the ex-spy engineered his own disappearance.
Jim Thompson, an American architect and former World War II spy credited with reviving the Thai silk industry, vanished in Malaysia's Cameron Highlands on Easter Sunday 30 years ago.

What happened to him on the afternoon of March 27, 1967 when he left his bungalow in the hills of central Malaysia and went for a stroll in the jungle has been the subject of a couple of books, numerous magazine articles and endless speculation since.

"I think he himself vanished to escape somewhere," said John Cheah, executive chef at the Smokehouse hotels and restaurants. "He was a spy. He used to be a mountain guerrilla, so how could he get lost?"
Cheah was working for a British army holiday bungalow next to the one Thompson was staying that Sunday afternoon and later that evening was among the hundreds who took part in the search.
TWO-WEEK SEARCH
"We searched until nightfall and it continued for almost a fortnight after that," Cheah told Reuters in an interview.
Local aborigines, known as orang asli (the original people) combed the thick jungle. Malay witchdoctors and Thai fortune tellers were enlisted but never found a trace of the man.

During World War Two, Thompson was a member of the U.S. army intelligence wing known as the Office of Stratetgic Services, a precursor to the Central Intelligence Agency (CIA). He received jungle training at the end of the war in Sri Lanka.
HEAVY SMOKER
But at the time of his disappearance he was in his early 60s, a heavy smoker and suffering from gallstones, said his biographer William Warren.
"He wasn't in the best of health. In fact, he had gone down there (Cameron Highlands) to rest," said Warren, who met Thompson a few days before the trip to discuss a book project.
Warren, a retired professor of literature who has lived in Thailand since 1960, said in a telephone interview from Bangkok he thinks Thompson got lost and his body has never been found.
"He was interested in plants and walking. I can imagine him taking one trail, then taking another trail and then another and then getting turned around."
Warren said no one who knew Thompson believed he was a spy, because his prominence in Bangkok society at the time would have been inconsistent with the cloak and dagger world of espionage.
He also dismissed the idea that Thompson somehow conjured up his own disappearance.

"It would have been easier to run away from Bangkok or anywhere else for that matter," Warren said. "He didn't have his passport, identification or anything when he went on that walk. It didn't look like he planned his escape and if it was planned by somebody else, how did they know where he would be?"
SWASHBUCKLING ADVENTURER
Part of the allure to this story is that Thompson, the swashbuckling adventurer and art collector, vanished at a time of intrigue in Southeast Asia when the Vietnam War was at its height.

An Indonesian general by the name of Suharto had just edged aside the late Sukarno to become acting President of Indonesia after brutally crushing a communist movement blamed for an abortive coup two years earlier.
Malaysia was still fighting the remnants of a communist insurgency in the jungles -- Thompson's kidnapping by guerrillas is still a popular theory.
Warren says the "total mystery" surrounding Thompson's disappearance is part of its fascination.
"Total mysteries are very rare. When somebody like Jimmy Hoffa disappeared, we know that he was probably murdered and sunk in concerete someplace. But here it's a complete mystery."

Several years ago, a skeleton was found not far from where Thompson vanished. It was front-page news in Malaysia amid speculation that it was Thompson's. But medical tests determined it was the body of a non-caucasian.
Thompson's home in Bangkok, which combines six traditional Thai teak buildings some two centuries old with its art collection still intact, still draws some 400 visitors a day.
FOUNDED SILK COMPANY

When Thompson arrived in Bangkok at the end of World War II, the silk industry had all but died in Thailand. The company he started, Jim Thompson Thai Silk Company, prospers today, mainly owned by a cooperative of weavers, Warren said.
The hand woven silk fabrics the company designed became internationally famous in the late 1940s and were used in the stage version of "The King and I".
